h1: The 6 Best NAS for Small Businesses of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best NAS for Small Businesses: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six NAS units for small businesses, from 2-bay starters to 4-bay Synology and UGREEN models, with software and RAID notes.
summary: The Synology DS925+ is our top pick for teams that expect to grow. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus gives four bays and a stronger CPU for less. The UGREEN DXP2800 is the budget starter, the Synology DS725+ starts small with an upgrade path, and the QNAP TS-264 is the pick if you prefer QNAP software.
intro: Buying a NAS for a small business usually goes wrong at the drive bay count. Two bays feel enough on day one, but a mirrored pair only gives you the capacity of a single drive, and the first time the team outgrows it you are migrating data under pressure.

We reviewed eight listings and dropped the WD Red Plus drive because it is a component rather than a NAS, though it appears in the advice below. Ranking weighs bay count, software, CPU and RAM where listed, RAID options, expandability and price bucket. This is a spec sheet comparison and carries no benchmark claims.

products.name: Synology 4-Bay DiskStation DS925+ (Diskless)
products.verdict: Four bays, mature software and the most room to grow.
products.description:
The DS925+ is a four bay diskless NAS running Synology DSM, with directory sync support and multi-bay RAID for redundancy. It is a plus-tier model eligible for business support and can be expanded as storage needs grow.

It ranks first because it combines headroom with the most polished software of the group. It sits in the $500 and up bucket, above the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus, which is the price of that ecosystem.

It suits a small business planning for team growth. The caveat is that drives are sold separately and add to the total.
products.idealFor: Growing teams that need room and support.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP4800 Plus 4-Bay NAS
products.verdict: Four bays and a five core Pentium Gold for less than Synology.
products.description:
The DXP4800 Plus is a four bay diskless NAS with an Intel Pentium Gold 8505 five core CPU, RAID across all bays and cloud backup integration. UGREEN positions it at a value tier against premium four bay rivals.

It ranks second because it matches the DS925+ on bay count while undercutting it on cost, though it has a younger software ecosystem. Both sit in the $500 and up bucket.

Buy it for CPU strength per dollar. The caveat is that drives are not included.
products.idealFor: Teams wanting strong CPU on a tighter budget.

products.name: Synology DS725+ Expandable NAS Storage (2-Bay, Diskless)
products.verdict: Start with two bays and expand without replacing it.
products.description:
The DS725+ is a two bay diskless NAS that can be expanded, with plus-tier support eligibility, private cloud storage and directory sync through DSM.

It ranks third because two bays limit redundancy to a mirrored pair, while the DS925+ offers more headroom. It sits in the $500 and up bucket, so it costs the same as larger rivals.

It works for a small office that wants a path to grow. The caveat is paying a premium for a two bay unit.
products.idealFor: Small offices planning to expand later.

products.name: QNAP TS-264-8G-US 2-Bay Desktop NAS
products.verdict: A two bay desktop NAS with 8GB RAM already installed.
products.description:
The TS-264 is a two bay desktop NAS with 8GB of RAM included, running the QNAP QTS software with directory sync and cloud backup support.

It ranks fourth because it lacks the expandability emphasis of the DS725+, but it includes more memory out of the box. It sits in the $200-500 bucket.

It suits teams who already prefer QNAP software. The caveat is that two bays cap redundancy.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP2800 2-Bay
products.verdict: An entry-level two bay unit with RAID 1 mirroring.
products.description:
The DXP2800 is a two bay diskless NAS aimed at creators and small teams, with gigabit networking and RAID 1 mirroring at an entry price.

It ranks fifth because gigabit networking is standard rather than fast and it offers fewer growth options. It sits in the $200-500 bucket.

It is a good first NAS for a solo business. The caveat is the limit on expansion.
products.skipIf: You expect to outgrow two bays.

products.name: Synology DS423 Family & Business Backup (4-Bay, Diskless)
products.verdict: A value-tier four bay for backup and surveillance.
products.description:
The DS423 is a four bay diskless value-tier Synology with support for video surveillance storage, a photo vault and secure file sharing.

It ranks last because it is a value model with fewer team features than the plus-tier DS925+. It sits in the $200-500 bucket, the lowest for four bays.

It suits small offices combining backup and cameras. The caveat is lighter business tooling.

whatMatters.detail: Each bay holds one drive. A mirrored pair gives you the space of one drive, while four bays allow parity setups with more usable space. Count the bays and decide what RAID level you want.
RAID spreads or copies data across drives so one failure does not lose files. RAID 1 mirrors two drives. Check the listing for supported RAID types, and remember RAID is not a backup.
The operating system decides how easy it is to set up users, shares and backups. Synology DSM, QNAP QTS and UGREEN differ in polish. Read what features the listing names.
These affect how well the NAS handles several users and apps at once. A listed CPU model and RAM figure are good signs. Look for them in the bullets.
Diskless means no drives are included. Use drives rated for NAS use, such as the WD Red Plus 8TB with CMR recording. Budget for the drives on top of the enclosure.

howToChoose.intro: Headcount and growth set how many bays you need.

cards.label: Synology
cards.text: Mature DSM software and business support. The DS925+, DS725+ and DS423 are Synology.

cards.label: UGREEN
cards.text: More hardware for the money, with a newer software platform. The DXP4800 Plus and DXP2800 are UGREEN.

howToChoose.note: Most small businesses should default to Synology unless CPU power per dollar is the top priority.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Simple setup software, RAID support and a clear path to add drives later.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Synology DS725+ pairs DSM with an expansion path, and the DXP2800 lowers the entry cost.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your team will grow, where the DS925+ gives four bays and business support.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Only a few people share files, where the DXP2800 or TS-264 is enough.

faq.q: Do these NAS units include hard drives?
faq.a: No. The Synology and UGREEN models are diskless, so you buy drives separately.

faq.q: Is RAID the same as a backup?
faq.a: No. RAID protects against a drive failure but not deletion or fire. Keep a separate backup copy.
Use NAS-rated drives, such as the WD Red Plus 8TB, which is built for continuous operation.
For a small team, yes. A mirrored pair gives one drive of usable space, so plan capacity accordingly.

faq.q: How do I connect staff to the NAS?
faq.a: Join it to your network, create user accounts and set shared folders. Directory sync helps if you use a central login.

faq.q: Can I move drives to a new NAS later?
faq.a: Often within the same brand, but check compatibility. Back up first.

finalTake: The Synology DS925+ is the NAS we would buy for a business that expects to grow. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus gives similar capacity for less, and the DXP2800 is a sensible entry. Whatever you choose, budget for NAS-rated drives and a separate backup.
